Lattice contribution to the electronic self-energy in complex correlated oxides is a fascinating subject that has lately stimulated lively discussions. Expectations of electron-phonon self-energy effects for simpler materials, such as Pd and Al, have resulted in several misconceptions in strongly correlated oxides. Here we analyze a number of arguments claiming that phonons cannot be the origin of certain self-energy effects seen in high-$T_c$ cuprate superconductors via angle resolved photoemission experiments (ARPES), including the temperature dependence, doping dependence of the renormalization effects, the inter-band scattering in the bilayer systems, and impurity substitution. We show that in light of experimental evidences and detailed simulations, these arguments are not well founded.

outputs.L2: The role of lattice vibrations in the electronic self-energy of complex, strongly correlated oxides has recently become the focus of considerable debate. Applying expectations derived from simpler metals, including palladium and aluminum, to these materials has led to several mistaken assumptions. We examine claims that phonons cannot account for specific self-energy features observed in high-\(T_c\) cuprate superconductors by angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES). outputs.L3:
The role of lattice vibrations in the electronic self-energy of complex correlated oxides remains a subject of active debate. In particular, interpretations of angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) measurements often rely on expectations derived from comparatively simple metals, such as palladium and aluminum. Applying these conventional expectations directly to strongly correlated oxides, however, can lead to misleading conclusions because these materials exhibit more complicated electronic structures, interactions, and screening behavior.

A central issue is whether phonons can account for the self-energy features observed by ARPES in high-temperature cuprate superconductors. Several arguments have been advanced against a phononic explanation. These include the reported temperature and doping dependence of the spectral features, the apparent role of interband scattering in bilayer cuprates, and changes produced by impurity substitution. Such observations have sometimes been interpreted as evidence that the relevant self-energy effects must arise primarily from electronic collective modes rather than from coupling between electrons and the lattice.

Closer examination, however, shows that these arguments do not rule out a phonon origin. Experimental findings, together with detailed simulations that account for the distinctive electronic and structural properties of the cuprates, demonstrate that electron-phonon coupling can produce behavior consistent with the observed temperature, doping, bilayer, and impurity trends. Consequently, conclusions based on analogies with simple metals or on overly restrictive models of electron-phonon interaction are not sufficiently robust. The available evidence instead supports the view that lattice effects may make a substantial contribution to the electronic self-energy in high-temperature cuprate superconductors.
outputs.L4:
Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) has revealed pronounced structures in the electronic dispersion and self-energy of high-\(T_c\) cuprate superconductors. These include the well-known nodal “kink,” changes in quasiparticle linewidth, and peak–dip–hump structures near the antinodal region. Such observations are widely interpreted as evidence that charge carriers interact strongly with collective excitations. The identity of those excitations, however, remains controversial. Magnetic modes are often favored, while phonons are sometimes dismissed on the grounds that several experimental trends appear incompatible with a lattice-based mechanism.

This text critically examines the main arguments used to exclude phonons. Particular attention is given to the temperature dependence of ARPES spectra, especially changes that occur near the superconducting transition temperature. The sharpening or redistribution of spectral features below \(T_c\) is frequently attributed to a magnetic resonance that develops in the superconducting state. Yet this interpretation is not unique. When the opening of an anisotropic superconducting gap, the energy dependence of the electronic density of states, finite quasiparticle lifetimes, experimental resolution, and realistic electron–phonon coupling are included, phonon-induced self-energy structures can also change substantially across \(T_c\). Consequently, the temperature evolution of a kink or peak–dip–hump feature does not by itself identify the bosonic excitation responsible for it.

The doping dependence of the spectra is examined in the same way. It has been argued that the persistence of certain ARPES anomalies over a broad doping range conflicts with a magnetic origin or, alternatively, that their correlation with superconducting properties rules out phonons. Both conclusions rely on an oversimplified picture. In strongly correlated materials, the measured self-energy depends not only on the bare boson spectrum but also on the evolving electronic structure, screening, quasiparticle coherence, superconducting gap, and momentum-dependent interaction vertex. A phonon may remain at nearly the same energy while the magnitude and line shape of its electronic signature vary strongly with doping. Conversely, changes in a self-energy feature need not imply that the underlying bosonic mode itself has changed by the same amount.

Bilayer cuprates provide another frequently cited objection. Their bonding and antibonding bands permit both intraband and interband scattering, and some analyses claim that the observed self-energies require a mode with a particular symmetry, such as an odd magnetic resonance. Detailed simulations show that this inference is not decisive. Once bilayer splitting, matrix-element effects, momentum-dependent coupling, superconducting coherence factors, and the available phase space for scattering are treated consistently, phonon-mediated processes can generate distinct structures in the bonding and antibonding spectra. Interband scattering is therefore not an exclusive signature of magnetic coupling, and ARPES intensity differences between the two bands cannot be interpreted without accounting for the full multiband electronic structure.

Impurity-substitution experiments are also reconsidered. Changes caused by replacing copper or other lattice ions have sometimes been presented as evidence against a phonon explanation, particularly when substitution suppresses superconductivity or modifies a magnetic resonance. Such impurities, however, affect several properties simultaneously. They introduce elastic scattering, broaden quasiparticle states, alter local electronic correlations, disturb the lattice, and can modify both magnetic and vibrational excitations. Simulated spectra demonstrate that impurity-induced broadening and loss of coherence can weaken or obscure a phonon-related self-energy feature even when the underlying electron–phonon interaction remains substantial. The disappearance of a sharp ARPES anomaly after substitution therefore does not establish that the original feature was magnetic.

Taken together, the experimental comparisons and numerical modeling show that the commonly cited anti-phonon arguments are not conclusive. This does not imply that magnetic fluctuations are absent or unimportant, nor does it establish that phonons alone account for superconductivity in the cuprates. Rather, it shows that the ARPES data are compatible with a significant lattice contribution to the electronic self-energy. In strongly correlated oxides, lattice vibrations, electronic correlations, magnetism, and superconductivity are intertwined, so attempts to assign spectral features to a single class of excitations must be made with caution. A realistic description of the cuprates should therefore allow for substantial, momentum-dependent electron–phonon coupling alongside other many-body interactions.

### Here

Between what we hope for and what becomes real, there is a lattice: a delicate structure built from plans, memories, and possibilities. We climb it carefully, carrying our expectations like baskets filled with uncertain fruit.

Yet life does not always wait at the top. Sometimes it is here—in the quiet space between one step and the next, in the light passing through the lattice, in the moment before expectation hardens into disappointment or blooms into surprise.

To be here is not to abandon hope. It is to loosen our grip on the future and notice what already surrounds us. The lattice may guide our growth, and expectations may give us direction, but only the present can be touched.

Here is where life happens.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a paper arguing that electron-phonon coupling can explain ARPES self-energy effects in high-\(T_c\) cuprate superconductors.
counterfactuals.output: **Abstract—** Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) of high-\(T_c\) cuprate superconductors reveals pronounced quasiparticle dispersion kinks, linewidth anomalies, and spectral-weight redistribution that provide direct information about the electronic self-energy. We show that these features can be consistently explained by electron–phonon coupling when the momentum dependence of the cuprate electronic structure, superconducting gap, and relevant lattice modes is treated explicitly. Calculations based on an anisotropic Migdal–Eliashberg framework reproduce the characteristic energy scales and momentum dependence of the nodal and antinodal self-energies, including the nodal kink near the oxygen-mode energies and the stronger renormalization below \(T_c\). The same framework accounts qualitatively for observed temperature, doping, and isotope dependences, while remaining compatible with realistic coupling strengths inferred from experiment and first-principles estimates. These results demonstrate that phonons can make a substantial—and in some regimes dominant—contribution to the ARPES self-energy without excluding additional electronic interactions. Electron–phonon coupling should therefore be included in any quantitative description of quasiparticle dynamics and pairing phenomenology in the cuprates.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize why common objections to a phononic origin of quasiparticle renormalization in correlated oxides are not well founded, addressing temperature, doping, bilayer interband scattering, and impurity substitution.
counterfactuals.output:
Common arguments against a phonon-based explanation of quasiparticle renormalization in correlated oxides are not decisive:

- **Temperature:** A phonon-induced kink or peak–dip–hump need not disappear at \(T_c\). Phonons exist above \(T_c\), while superconductivity mainly sharpens their electronic self-energy signature by reducing damping and opening a gap. Thermal broadening can weaken the feature smoothly. Thus changes near \(T_c\) do not uniquely imply a superconductivity-induced magnetic resonance.

- **Doping:** Nearly doping-independent kink energies are natural for lattice modes, whose frequencies vary much less than electronic or magnetic scales. Changes in kink strength with doping can arise from altered screening, quasiparticle coherence, density of states, and superconducting-gap size. In the superconducting state, the observed structure often occurs near \(\Omega_{\rm ph}+\Delta\), so apparent energy shifts need not reflect a changing boson frequency.

- **Bilayer interband scattering:** Interband scattering between bonding and antibonding bands is not unique to an odd magnetic mode. Bilayer phonons also have even and odd symmetry and can obey the same parity selection rules, including strong bonding–antibonding scattering. Moreover, similar renormalizations in single-layer compounds undermine an explanation that requires bilayer magnetic scattering.

- **Impurity substitution:** Zn, Ni, or other substitutions modify far more than magnetism: they broaden electronic states, suppress quasiparticle coherence and the superconducting gap, change local bonding, and perturb phonons and screening. Consequently, the weakening or reshaping of a self-energy feature after substitution cannot by itself identify the mediating boson. The persistence of renormalization even when magnetic collective modes are strongly suppressed can instead favor a lattice contribution.

Overall, these observations do not prove that phonons are solely responsible, but they do show that temperature, doping, bilayer symmetry, and impurity trends are compatible with substantial—and sometimes dominant—electron–phonon coupling.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a concise research-paper abstract about lattice contributions to electronic self-energy in complex correlated oxides, contrasting cuprates with simpler metals such as Pd and Al.
counterfactuals.output: We investigate lattice contributions to the electronic self-energy in complex correlated oxides, emphasizing their distinction from conventional metals. In Pd and Al, phonon-induced renormalization is generally well described by Migdal–Eliashberg theory, producing modest, mode-specific features governed by the electron–phonon coupling strength. Cuprates instead exhibit broad, momentum- and doping-dependent self-energy anomalies superimposed on strong electronic correlations, complicating the separation of lattice and purely electronic effects. Comparative analysis indicates that phonons contribute measurably to quasiparticle mass enhancement and dispersion kinks in cuprates, but their signatures are reshaped by anisotropic electronic structure, reduced screening, and competing spin and charge fluctuations. Thus, lattice coupling in correlated oxides cannot be inferred directly from conventional-metal benchmarks; it must be treated within a framework that incorporates both electron–phonon interactions and strong many-body correlations.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an academic paragraph defending electron-phonon interpretations of ARPES anomalies in high-\(T_c\) cuprates using experimental evidence and detailed simulations.
counterfactuals.output: Electron–phonon coupling provides a compelling explanation for several prominent anomalies observed by angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) in high-\(T_c\) cuprates. Most notably, the ubiquitous \(50\!-\!80\) meV “kink” in the nodal dispersion occurs near the energies of oxygen bond-stretching and related lattice modes measured by neutron and Raman spectroscopy, while corresponding changes in quasiparticle linewidth are consistent with the opening of phonon-emission channels. Reports of oxygen-isotope-dependent shifts in the kink and associated high-energy spectral features further implicate lattice dynamics, because such shifts follow the expected mass dependence of phonon frequencies and are not naturally produced by a purely electronic boson. In addition, ARPES self-energies often contain fine structure that tracks peaks in the experimentally determined phonon density of states. Detailed simulations based on anisotropic, multiband Migdal–Eliashberg theory—using realistic dispersions, momentum-dependent electron–phonon matrix elements, multiple optical phonon branches, experimental resolution, and superconducting-gap effects—can reproduce the observed dispersion renormalization, peak–dip–hump line shapes, linewidth changes, and their temperature and momentum dependence without requiring anomalously large coupling constants. Although magnetic excitations may contribute, especially in antinodal regions, the agreement among phonon energy scales, isotope effects, independent vibrational measurements, and realistic spectral-function calculations demonstrates that electron–phonon interactions are a substantial, and in some regimes dominant, source of cuprate ARPES anomalies.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain, in the style of a condensed-matter physics article abstract, how misconceptions based on simple materials have shaped debates over phonon-induced self-energy effects in strongly correlated oxides.
counterfactuals.output: Debates over phonon-induced electronic self-energies in strongly correlated oxides have often been framed by intuition inherited from weakly correlated, nearly free-electron metals. In that setting, Migdal–Eliashberg theory associates electron–phonon coupling with comparatively modest mass renormalization, phonon-scale dispersion kinks, and linewidth changes constrained by a well-defined Fermi surface and efficient screening. Applied uncritically to cuprates and related oxides, these expectations fostered several misconceptions: that large spectral anomalies cannot be phononic, that a kink energy uniquely identifies a bosonic mode, and that weak isotope shifts or transition-temperature effects imply negligible coupling. Strong correlations instead redistribute spectral weight, reduce screening, amplify momentum and orbital selectivity, and can invalidate simple quasiparticle and adiabatic assumptions; electronic collective modes may also hybridize with lattice excitations. Consequently, phonons can produce pronounced, doping-dependent self-energy signatures without obeying textbook relations between coupling strength, linewidth, isotope response, and pairing. Conversely, correlation-generated anomalies can mimic phonon signatures, making dispersion alone non-diagnostic. A consistent interpretation therefore requires joint analysis of energy, momentum, temperature, doping, and isotope dependence within theories that treat Coulomb correlations and lattice coupling on comparable footing, replacing the false dichotomy of “electronic” versus “phononic” mechanisms with an explicitly intertwined description.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
